Ireland’s Electrical Equipment Industry Reports Steady Growth Amid Stable Demand

DUBLIN, June 24 — Ireland’s electrical equipment industry posted steady growth in the first quarter of 2024, buoyed by resilient domestic demand and ongoing investment in renewable energy and infrastructure, the Irish Association of Electrical Manufacturers (IAEM) said Monday.

Industry revenue rose 5.2% year-on-year to EUR 1.47 billion for the quarter ending March 31, according to IAEM estimates, with strong performance in the power transmission, switchgear, and smart metering segments. Export sales accounted for nearly 60% of total revenue, reflecting solid demand from EU markets, particularly Germany, France, and the Netherlands.

“The industry has benefited from robust construction activity and continued upgrades to the national grid,” said Aoife Coughlan, IAEM chief executive. “Irish manufacturers are also capitalising on the transition to green energy and digitalisation, with significant orders for smart equipment coming from both public and private sectors.”

Major players reported modest but consistent increases in order books. Keltor Electric, one of the country’s largest electrical equipment suppliers, said its quarterly sales rose 4.8% from a year earlier, driven by contracts in commercial real estate and renewable energy projects. “We are seeing strong interest in our energy-efficient systems as more businesses prioritise sustainability,” said Keltor CEO Brian O’Shea.

Smaller firms also reported positive trends, citing demand for building automation and advanced lighting solutions. “There’s healthy appetite for innovation, especially in retrofitting older properties with smart controls,” said Maeve Quinn, managing director of Liffey Circuits.

Employment in the sector rose 2.1% compared to the same period last year, with IAEM data showing 13,800 people directly employed in manufacturing and related services. According to SIPTU, the largest union representing technical workers, wage growth kept pace with inflation, and there were no major industrial disputes during the quarter.

Analysts said the sector’s outlook remained positive, but noted that challenges persist. “Ireland’s electrical equipment industry is well-placed to benefit from EU climate targets and infrastructure spending,” said Conor Mullins, industry analyst at Iona Consulting. “However, firms are keeping a close eye on input costs and global supply chains, which remain volatile.”

The IAEM expects industry revenue to grow by 4–6% for the full year, provided current demand trends continue and supply chain conditions remain stable. “We are optimistic about the rest of 2024,” Coughlan said, “as Ireland continues to electrify and modernise its economy.”
